sentences.text: Revenue in the metrics table grew from $23.7 billion in FY2016 [F1] to $51.8 billion in FY2025 [F10], a 9.1% CAGR [F168], but the path was cyclical rather than compounding.
After a 58.0% fall in FY2020 [D161] to $13.7 billion [F5], revenue rose 153.2% in FY2021 [D200] and 76.5% in FY2022 [D238] to $61.0 billion [F7].
The FY2022 peak of $61.0 billion [F7] reflects higher realized prices and volumes, mainly from the Shell Permian acquisition [P59].
Revenue then fell 20.5% in FY2023 [D274] to $48.5 billion [F8], which the filing puts down to lower realized commodity prices, partly offset by higher volumes [P47].
In FY2025 Lower 48 contributed 8.0pp [D713] of the 7.6% growth in total segment revenue [D691] and made up 70.2% of segment revenue [D711].

Table revenue rose 4.9% to $51.8 billion [D342][F10]; the filing attributes the move to higher volumes, including Marathon Oil, and higher realized gas prices, partly offset by lower crude prices [P28].
Crude oil, 66.3% of disaggregated revenue [D551], grew only 0.1% [D552] and added 0.1pp [D553].
Income before income taxes fell from $13.7 billion [X90] to $12.7 billion [X91] while table revenue rose 4.9% [D342], so pre-tax profit moved opposite to revenue.
Basic EPS fell 18.7% [D344] against a 13.6% fall in net income [D343], and diluted shares rose 6.1% [D356], so per-share declines were larger.
Net margin was 15.4% [F30] against a 17.9% window median [D831] and a 30.6% high [D830], but above the energy peer median of 8.1% [D847].
Cost of revenue rose to 37.9% of revenue [D326] from 36.6% [D292], and DD&A to 19.5% [D330] from 17.5% [D296], which the filing ties to Marathon Oil [P22].
SG&A fell 22.9% [D354] as the prior year's Marathon Oil transaction expenses dropped out [P23].
The effective tax rate rose to 36.9% [D332] from 32.4% [D298], and the filings cited do not explain the move.
Operating cash flow of $19.8 billion [F59] was 2.48x net income [D333], above 1.82x in FY2023 [D265] and 2.18x in FY2024 [D299].
Cash flow fell 1.6% [D346] on lower commodity prices, mostly offset by Marathon Oil operations [P6].
In FY2022 free cash flow was 0.97x net income [D227] and 23.1% of revenue [D223], against a 12.2% window median [D834], with capex at 1.35x D&A [D228].
Operating cash flow rose 66.6% to $28.3 billion in FY2022 [D242][F56], which the filing ties to higher prices and volumes, partly offset by Libya and Norway tax payments [P52].
Net cash was $7.1 billion at FY2025 [D337], up from $6.1 billion in FY2024 [D303], or 12.1% of revenue [D338].
Against six energy peers, that net cash to revenue ranks at the 100th percentile [D850], versus a peer median of -7.7% [D851].
Total debt of $1.0 billion [D336] equals the current portion alone [X203], so net cash may omit noncurrent debt and the peer ranking needs checking.
Buybacks of $5.0 billion [X141] and dividends of $4.0 billion [X151] totalled $9.0 billion [D339], which the filing puts at 46 percent of operating cash flow [P31].
Liquidity was adequate but below its window median, with a current ratio of 1.30x [F153] against 1.45x [D843].
Table revenue differs from as-reported revenue every year, for example $51.8 billion [F10] against $58.9 billion [X10] in FY2025, so growth figures here are table-on-table only.
Net income fell 41.3% [D275], 15.6% [D309] and 13.6% [D343] in FY2023 to FY2025, and the filing ties FY2025 pressure to Marathon Oil DD&A and production costs [P17].
Diluted shares rose 6.1% in FY2025 [D356], to 1,253.4m [X131] from 1,180.9m [X130], and the filings cited do not explain the increase.
The earnings decline looks like normalisation from the FY2022 peak net margin of 30.6% [F27] rather than an accelerating loss.
Net margin staying below the 17.9% window median [D831] from 15.4% [F30] would confirm the trend; a return above 17.9% would reverse it, per the FY2026 10-K.
Diluted shares above 1,253.4m [X131] would confirm the dilution; a count below it would show buybacks catching up, per the FY2026 10-K.
Reaching the $5 billion disposition target by year-end 2026 [P32] tests asset-sale funding for returns; missing it would weaken that funding, per the FY2026 10-K.
